utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We won't keep you long this afternoon. Mr. Krsnik, your re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you, I'll be very brief. Could the witness be shown Exhibit 743.1 and 734?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, would you please be kind enough to examine document 743.1? It is the alleged report on the handover of detainees. Would you first be kind to check the left, upper angle, where the reference number should be written? Does the number feature there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At the bottom, it says, "Official." What does it say underneath that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are the initials PM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's M, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is there a seal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The last question concerning this document, could you tell us where you were located on the 29th of January, 1994? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the 2nd Guard's Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have any function to perform there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should go into private session for these questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the restructuring and reorganisation took place somewhere before the start of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us when formally you ceased to exist? That is the ATG Krusko -- Krusko unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We ceased to exist formally in December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you now please look at the second document? The upper left corner, what is the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 2nd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The name under item 6, could you tell us when, possibly the year and the month, this person was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date. It was December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Would you also -- my last question -- tell us whether, in the lower right angle where it says "commander," you can see whose signature is under this heading "commander" and whether there is a seal as well on this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whose signature this is, and there is no seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I have no further questions for you. Thank you for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, I won't keep you long but I have a few questions for you. You were telling us yesterday that Juka Prazina left in June of 1993. He went to the sea, I think you said. Did he just go on a holiday or did he quit being commander of the unit that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally believe that he went on a holiday. He would come back and he would call me and he would tell me before leaving to take his place. However, he never came back, he never called me again, and I told him that, later on, that we were waiting for him, but he didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you say you told him you were waiting for him, did you actually speak to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with him. He told me that, since his wife was severely injured in Sarajevo, she was accommodated somewhere on the seaside and he told me that he would go to the sea for that purpose and that he would come back, but he never came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I move on to a different issue, on the day -- on the days of the 9th and 10th of May, when the major conflict occurred in Mostar and the Vranica building was the focus of fighting, you gave testimony to the effect that because your women and children were at risk, a number of you stayed behind to guard them in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, I thought on two occasions that was what your testimony was. Can you correct me, if I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I'd like to repeat what I said yesterday. Perhaps you didn't understand me well, so with your permission, Your Honour, I'd like to repeat what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before May 9 and 10, a few days earlier, I was wounded, I went to the hospital, and then I was dismissed. I had a wound, gun wound, gunshot wound, in my left heel. In that morning, on the 9th of May, when Juka, the commander, at about 9.00 or 10.00 a.m. Left, he told me that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had launched an attack, that he had to leave and be -- become -- and join the reserve unit Ludvig Pavlovic. I stayed in the Heliodrom myself because I had been wounded, and I couldn't join him. And together with me, there were some ten other men who were in the Heliodrom, and there were also women and children there. My wife was also there. She was pregnant at that time. And having undergone the events in the Igman together with my wife, had the BH Army not arrived there, and having had this experience from Mount Igman, I decided to stay in the Heliodrom. Furthermore I was also wounded and I couldn't leave. This is what I said yesterday. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we won't argue about that. But that is essentially what I understood you to have said, and I thought I said. But however, can I take it from that that you had two reasons for staying behind? One, your injury, and secondly the protection of your loved ones? The question that I want to follow from that was can we take it that the commander of your unit left with a number of combatants? In other words, most of the unit left the Heliodrom with him, to go on duty, to assist, as you said, the Ludvig Pavlovic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that clarifies that for me. I want to go to it a different subject now. Were you, as a soldier in the unit, paid each week or each month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know who paid you and where you were paid? In other words, did you have to go somewhere to collect your weekly or monthly pay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of us always, when there was the monthly pay, had to go and collect them from the Grude logistical centre. This is where the monthly pays were disbursed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: One of you would go to Grude. Were you paid with an envelope with a cash with a pay slip? Did you have to sign any documents? Did that person bring a list which all of you had could countersign? Was there any documentary procedure for obtaining your salary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a certain period of time, we were paid in cash and we had to countersign a document. And later on, we received pay slips and everybody personally had to go to a bank or somewhere to collect the pay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know by whom you were paid, apart from the fact that one of your colleagues went to Grude to collect the money and then -- but do you know which institution paid you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institution that paid us was the Main Staff. We were subordinate to the Main Staff, and the Ministry of Defence was the institution of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, if I bring you to the period when you were the commander of the unit, when your commander had unfortunately been killed, did you have a procedure or protocol that you followed when one of your men was either injured or had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's really a follow through on payments. What procedure, if any, did you follow to ensure that somebody who had been killed was not receiving a salary? What was the protocol when somebody was killed or injured? First of all, tell me what you did and then I will have some follow-up questions in relation to your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, if you're referring to 1994, when we were receiving the pay in the guards brigade, when a soldier would be killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm referring to the unit that you belonged to with Juka Prazina after he left, that small unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, we were not paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you want to change your evidence on that? When I asked you how were you paid, you described how one of the staff would go to Grude and collect the money. Later on it became more streamlined and you got a pay slip and you went to the bank. Do you want to change that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I insist on my testimony. When we arrived there with Juka, and then when he had left, then somebody would go and collect our pay, would bring the pay and everybody would have to countersign a pay slip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Really what I want to know is now in the short period -- sorry, did I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What as far as the killed combatants are concerned, their families would receive their pay. And even today, I have very good relations with these families, because I live in Sarajevo and my family is in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So if somebody -- if somebody were killed in action, the same pay would be paid to his family? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Your Honours, if I may say, if such a person had a wife and a child, at that time, there was no welfare or any other care for these children to be taken care of, and this is how we did it. Just by way of example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Would the payment list of a unit, then, include the names of the soldiers who had died or would the dead soldiers' name be replaced by his widow or next-of-kin's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a very young commander at that time, and it was very difficult for me to take care of these families. Initially it was the killed soldier's name on the list, as far as I can recall it, and then either a member of his family or next of kin signed or sometimes I signed. As this has been going on over the last few years. If there was a disabled person, I would go and collect their pay in Sarajevo and take the pay to such a disabled person. This is my duty. This is a part of my honour that I feel to my former soldiers, and I try to help them, themselves, personally or their children, old and sick mothers, et cetera. This is my duty and my responsibility even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's very laudable and I congratulate you on carrying out your duty. The point I'm making is that because payment would be made to the next of kin of a soldier who was killed, that would explain the appearance of mothers and wives names on soldiers pay lists, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. It explains a lot. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, one thing to clarify about Juka Prazina. Was Juka Prazina, according to what you know, killed during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that I read it in the newspapers because over the last year or two, I've been working and living in Sarajevo, and I receive information through the newspapers after the war, that he was killed after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, it was reported in the newspapers and this was reported after the war. Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And isn't it true that he was killed in Belgium? Do you recall that from the media report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that. I have been in contact with the wife, and as far as -- and his daughter, whenever I can, of course I try to take care of them, be in contact with them. She told me, however, that he was buried in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: One other question: When you said that you received pay slips and that you had to collect the money of your wages from a bank, which bank would you collect that money from? Do you remember the name of the bank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall that it was the Mostarska Bank, Mostarska Banka Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one other question on Juka, and that will be my last question. Was Juka killed or was Juka murdered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rumours have it, and newspapers wrote it, that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how was he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one question with regard to Judge Clark's questions. You were talking exclusively about your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your killed combatants, could they further be kept on the soldier's pay list or did they have to be put on another list? Welfare list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received a list, and it was the same list for ATG Krusko, for both the -- those soldiers who were still alive and those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you had one list but the names were separated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because sometimes one of their relatives or I myself would sign and send them the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Witness, for coming to The Hague to help us. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. All of us wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we would just ask that the Exhibit P249 be admitted. It would have a Defence number of D1/411. Would that be right, Mrs. Registrar? Would that be the next number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I want to know whether this document has been admitted before or not, because it's the Prosecutor's document. Yes, Mr. Bos? Would you please enlighten us on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To my knowledge, this is a Prosecution exhibit which has already been admitted so I don't see the need to have it admitted again but if the Defence also wants to have it a Defence Exhibit number we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could have a different number to indicate it's also the document used by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought that was the proper procedure. D1/411, I think would be the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On the side of the Prosecution, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have two new exhibits to tender, Exhibit P623.1, which is Tuta's communication to Mr. Stampar dated 5 October, 1993. And Exhibit P706.1, which is the report on the incident in the Mostar hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections? Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. These are new documents. As far as 706.1 goes, I believe that the witness absolutely denied that incident happened or occurred whatsoever. So there would be no foundation for that. There is no probative value whatsoever. 623.1, also a new document. The witness testified he had never seen this paper before, didn't know about it. He said his name was on it but he didn't know about it, had never seen it, so there is no foundation, no probative value, nor is it relevant. So we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this Chamber will have to read this document and make our decision at a later stage. Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your next witness? I know you're always ready for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can see some light at the end of the tunnel, which makes me a bit better, and of course, I am ready. Now we are going to be dealing with experts, with scientists. So maybe we will learn something from them. I certainly believe it is going to be very interesting. My first witness is a witness for whom I don't need any protection measures. His name is Dr. Ante Markotic, a scientist. He is one of the most prominent demographers, a person who engages in demographic science, among the most prominent world experts in the field. We are ready. We are going to have some problems. I found it very difficult to understand him and that's why I asked him to be -- to use simple terms so that even lay persons can understand him. This is a very specific subject, very specific topic, and very specific science but I do believe it is going to prove very efficient and very relevant for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, thank you very much for your information. I think the last time you dealt with that witness pretty well. There is no need to ask a lot of questions to the expert witness because we already have their statements at our hands. I think what you have to do is to establish that witness, the qualification of this witness, and later on, draw our attention to certain points in his statement. I believe you quite understand that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honours. I have only five questions for this expert, just to start the discussion, and then I will hand him over to the Prosecution, but we have maps here that only he can explain. I have six maps here ready for the expert to explain, and then I have four questions to lay some foundation and then I'll be ready to hand the witness over to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, your direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We can keep the ELMO because we will need it for the maps. Are you feeling comfortable?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I could hardly recognise myself in the lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, just one piece of advice. We -- all you say is being translated into two languages. You do not speak fast any way but I'm going to kindly ask you to pause before you start giving your answers. We will start by you giving us your first and last name and then just briefly your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Can I start? Thank you very much. Ante F. Markotic born in village Grab, municipality of Ljubuski in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I finished education in Grab, Ljubuski, Capljina, Sarajevo, Zagreb, and in some other countries. I would like to point out my additional education in the Soviet Union, when I was -- had been given the grant of the United Nations. The subject was population and development. And at several European universities in Mannheim, Bratislava. Then I had inter-university cooperation with Granville University College in the United States of America, and on four or five occasions, I stayed and worked in Canada. I graduated from the university in Sarajevo. I defended my master's thesis and my Ph.D. in Zagreb and then I was in the Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia the United States and Canada. My field of expertise is demography and development that is population and regional development. What else can I say? Let me mention the functions that I had. One of them was at the school of economics of the University of Sarajevo. I was the deputy dean in 1980. Later on, I was the deputy mayor of the city of Sarajevo. That was in 1988. Later on, I was an expert at the London conference on the former Yugoslavia. Then I participated in the preparation of the Vance Owen plan for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina and I also participated in the Vienna talks on Bosnia-Herzegovina. Obviously my area of expertise is mostly, its population and regional development. Within that context at the end of my introduction, I would like to say that I have authored several books. Several proceedings, and some 130 scientific and expert papers in the field of demography and regional sciences. Thank you very much. If I have forgotten something, please remind me. Bear in mind I was born in the first half of the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I believe that you know your curriculum vitae best of all of us. In the beginning I would like to ask the usher to put this book on the ELMO, and my question is going to be very simple. Your expert's opinion has mostly been published in this book. Do I have your permission to translate it into English and give it to this Chamber as another piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my last book. I hope there will be more to follow. And it is a collection of my papers covering the period from the 1990s to the day of its publication. It consists of several very serious scientific contributions based on scientific procedure, and those who are the product of my previous knowledge and my dealing and looking at my homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, during the war, and those things that I participated in personally in order to find a solution to this tragic country. I would very much like to see this book read by others, and I would like to hear other people's opinion on it, but my work is the result of my engagement in this very broad aspect of work, but I'm not sure that this is the best summary of all that knowledge. I believe that there are people who could do it better. I'm talking about the summary of the book. So if any of you would be willing to do that, to the benefit of all, I would be much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this has entered the transcript. I have your permission to have it translated and I will tender that book as another exhibit. Let's move on. Mr. Professor, I have prepared five questions for you because everything else is in your expert findings. But in order to start, I would like to ask you the following: We are not experts for this topic but I would like to sort of speak in layman terms and I hope you will be able to help us understand your area of expertise. As far as I understand, you are the person who understands maps. Maps speak a lot more than words. But sometimes our laypersons do not understand maps. Let me give you Exhibit D1/402 to 1/405 -- 9, sorry, so let's start with your explanations. D1/402 to D1/409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have some problems with the numbers. I think I only have the D1/403.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 403 to 410, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I believe they are in chronological order but can you please check that for me? So let's deal with the maps in a chronological order?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Help me. How do you want me to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You are the author of all these maps and you know them best. In front of you is one map. I'm not?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on maps. I use them. In front of you, you have a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Professor. Can I interrupt you, please? I believe that you are speaking too fast. Can you please slow down? We have English interpretation and French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this map, there is a date and I worked in the -- at the school of economics when the occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina started, and I was deliberating on everything that had befallen us at the time. The longer I stayed there, the longer we were shelled, I published more and more contributions in the Sarajevo dailies. One of the maps in front of you is my attempt to mock all those who were in a position to do something and they didn't do anything. And the title of this map is, "Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1992." The subtitle is, "Where is the Bosnian ship sailing?" And I mean Bosnia and Herzegovina. And underneath, it says, "The representative of the international community. Upside-down Europe 1992, Cutilheiro without a compass." What was I implying? I was saying that some people arrived in this complex country, that they found it struck by tragic events, without having known anything about it, and if I had started complaining sooner, I would have sooner come to those who could have helped us. Now you see the black areas. This looks like the current federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is one of the Dayton, that is in the constitution of this land. The uncoloured areas are the ones with the predominant Serbian population. The darker colour, the stronger the attacks. You can see here Foca, Srebrenica, Konjic, Ravno, Kupres and municipalities in the Bosnian Posavina. That is Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I apologise. So there are no names of municipalities but the darker the colour, the bigger the tragedy. An additional part of this map, which I can't see on my screen too well is my attempt to play with the names of municipalities. There is some there is the Cyrillic script, there is Latinic script. There are combinations of the two, and all that is within the context of the events that were already taking place in the neighbouring Republic of Croatia. Whatever is happening in Croatia, I call it the nursery of the tragedy or the kindergarten of the tragedy that will later on move to the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Obviously I had to say that what it says here, but is not complete, where is the delivery room of that tragedy? I'm not hiding it from you today. I didn't hide it from the public at that time. I put the delivery room of the tragedy in Serbia. That's what I thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, can you please slow down? I had to kindly ask to you slow down. We have all the time in the world but you have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You are speaking so fast that the interpreters are finding very difficult to interpret you and then your message will be lost. For the transcript, and our interpreters -- you are making the lives of the interpreters very hard.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I'll try to slow down. Even then, I thought today I'm convinced that my predictions were very accurate. So the delivery room of the tragedy was in the east, in Serbia. The tragedy was tested, the testing ground was Croatia. That was in 1992. And the trauma struck in the today's republic, Republika Srpska. At the time it was still the so-called Republika Srpska. The death was in the black municipalities. The dust was in Foca. Today it is a part of Serbia. The map depicts another interesting area called -- or the title called, "1991 in the part of the then municipality of Trebinje," which was -- which used to be Ravno municipality, and when the war started, the population was mostly Croat population. Then that municipality became part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You can see the year here, 1991. Even to this very day, we cannot agree in my homeland where the war started and how the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So much for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's move on to the second map which bears number 404.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Here there is another map of mine. This was published officially in Oslobodjenja which was published in Sarajevo, this was published on the 7th of June, 1992. The text next to the map is not mine. I'm not the author of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to assist, I ask for clarification myself and perhaps it would assist the Chamber this appears to be what's on the overhead marked as Exhibit 410, not 404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My mistake. Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor for your help. So we are indeed looking at the Exhibit number 410.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please continue?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Unlike the previous map, this map is official because it was published in the daily paper. This can be checked. This was my personal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reaction to the developments, but there is no big difference between this map and the previous map. But in this map, those who published it, to illustrate the text, recognised in this map the reality of that moment. The black colour here shows municipalities with the predominant Serbian municipalities or better say municipalities where the Serbian population prevailed. Again, the darker the colour, the more Serbian population in the municipality. However, look at the brighter areas, the lighter areas, which represent those municipalities where the Muslim and Croat population prevailed. I used to call them Muslim and I still call them Muslim population. I am using the term that was -- that are the basis for my analysis in -- based on the official statistics today, census is going to show something else. This is not a deliberate error. This is just an attempt to provide an official interpretation for the name of the constituent people who in the meantime have changed their name and today call themselves Bosniaks. However, the same message of the author of the text and my message is as follows: The white municipalities, so to say, are more or less attacked municipalities. Then and today, I am saying that, after ten years, we can recognise the intention of the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina. The question can be asked at this point: Why were the municipalities with the predominant Croatian and Muslim population were attacked? I don't want to give you any answers. This is the map that illustrates the facts of the time. I don't want to impose my conclusions on you. I will leave it to you to conclude for yourselves. However, there is no coincidence that at the time in the early 1990s, in 1991, 1992, the war was waged in the areas which did not have a predominant Serbian population, whereas the areas where the predominant Serbian population areas were war-free. And this is where I would like to stop commenting on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we understand that you are eager to give your evidence, but I have to tell you that you speak really too fast, which gives a difficult time to the interpretation. Please be sure to make a pause after each sentence. You have to understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to understand that whatever you say will be translated into the other two languages. Thank you very much. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, the title of your expert work is as follows: "Bosnia and Herzegovina, the state between ethnic cleansing in peace and ethnic cleansing in war." Please, can you explain this heading, this title, to the Chamber? And please, can you look at the maps 405, 406, 407, 408 and 409?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: What I have said so far explains and draws your conclusion to the fact that my state is a very complex social entity. The complexity of it I tried to depict in the title of my expert work, and the title of my expert work, of my expertise, I hope, is clear to everybody. The message of that title is as follows: We have to know something about Bosnia and Herzegovina from previous times, when we are proposing arguments in very simple terms. One has to ask oneself: Why does Bosnia and Herzegovina look as it looks today? As for the constitution and the appearance of my country, I can say that I recognise the elements of its territorial complexity, which I would say has been present from its beginnings, and it has always been a bone in the throat of its development. Why do I say that? This was true during the period of Austro-Hungarian empire, during Yugoslavia, of both Yugoslavia, and it is still true today. When we are trying together with the international community to decipher, to find out a good, just solution for this country, for this country to be independent and to be able to develop independently, on its own. In my attempt to answer to my own question, as a human being, as a scientist, and the question that I'm trying to answer is as follows: Why does my country, in which all those who I remember were born, all those that my predecessors remember, how come that this country has not seen anything but tragedies over the past 100 years? And these tragedies cannot be compared to anything that the European civilisation has seen, after the first and Second World Wars. Unlike the rest of Europe, my homeland has seen the third world war in the 1990s. The appearance, the shape of my homeland, to me as a scientist who deals with people or in more sophisticated terms, who deals with the science on population, so this shape, this appearance, warns both you and me that this shape hides a lot of answers to my question. I would like to draw your attention to the indications in the previous two maps, where, to my mind, in this part, lies part of the question and part of the answer to this key human civilisational and, if you will, European question. Unfortunately, the question has not been limited to European border lines but by the force of its tragedy it has become a broader international issue. Finally, there are very few ethnical, cultural and areas or states as complex as Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is surprising that what happened happened in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, I apologise for the interruption. I believe that we have to narrow down your testimony. That's why I have given you these maps. Can you please sort them out in the chronological order and can you please use them in order to introduce the topic to the Honourable Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Okay. In front of you is a very colourful map. This is Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991. I am the author of the wall map and the name of this map is, "The ethnical map of Bosnia-Herzegovina." The part of the complexity of Bosnia-Herzegovina arises from its national composition. When I was researching this segment of the society in Bosnia and Herzegovina, under the conditions that -- in which this country developed, and one cannot ignore the ethnic facts, both in demographical terms, as well as in economic terms. But one also has to mention the ethnical, religious, social and other aspects of this country. One can also not ignore the tragical consequences of the First and Second World Wars, and especially one cannot ignore the fact that this state, as a part of Yugoslavia, in the -- in mid-20th century had one half of its population was illiterate. That is why all the terms that I have mentioning have to be put in that context, and deliberated on in that context. Before the war, the society did not bear that in mind. So when looking at the map today, I can say that rare are those people, even in scientific circles who could give you the exact national or ethnic structure of this state. Why is that so? There are several reasons for that. My profession is one of those who can provide you with some answers based on scientific data. This is very little, because a number of statistical data, and especially for the local and broader areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, professor, I again have to interrupt you. You have to slow down. I know that you will find it very hard to concentrate on what you want to say and say that slowly. You're not used to that. However, without that, we won't be able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: So when we are talking about the terms that you have already heard, one has to bear in mind that this is a complex state with a very low level of literacy, very low level of education, general culture, and that the country that was economically underdeveloped. That is why the demographic variances amongst the state-forming peoples are a particular sticking point in their relations. To my mind, when I was looking at the demographic side of the complexity of this country, the causes of the war and the relations have to be sought within this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, again, I apologise for the interruption. I don't mean to be rude. We are approaching our first break. Can you please be more specific? Can you start explaining the colours in the map?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: The colours do not make sense if you do not understand the context. I am not a cartographer. I do not draw maps. That's why I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. absolutely agree that every map -- this is just one more general remark and then I will concentrate on the maps. Every map depicting this area, this complex area, simplifies matter for everybody. The ethnical map, whose -- who -- that I have authored is the only one dating back from the Austro-Hungarian times. That is the only ethnical map that covers the area between 1910 and 1990. And that in the country which is so complex. That is why I would like to say that my fellow citizens, regardless of their ethnical origin, that they were very much ethnically illiterate. The ethnical map of this country can be metaphorically explained by saying that it gives just the basic data for those who are not experts in the area. This is just like an identity card which gives the country the name, the first and the last name, and the date of birth, but if you want to know more about the country, you have to have more background information. Why am I speaking in such tiny detail? I'm speaking in this tiny detail because such maps can be manipulated. And when you manipulate the larger masses, which do not understand anything, then it suffices for you to show them one colour. Just to illustrate this, you may not be able to find it, Kalinovik is a municipality south of Sarajevo. It is much bigger in size than any of the municipalities within the city of Sarajevo. However municipalities of Sarajevo proper are much more densely populated than Kalinovik municipality. A half illiterate or illiterate person will see the colour but will not understand the essence. That's why maps like this on their own serve more to confuse than to explain things to a lay person. That is why I, in a certain way, can be the one who has tried to deceive the general public. But I didn't. My wall map had a lot of additional information which then served to explain the things that may have been confusing. Look at the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina which in 1991 was the way it was. This was the reflection of the situation in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break, Witness. We have to break here. Mr. Krsnik, as you said that compared with this witness we are all laymen so I guess this witness could not be misled by specific questions so after the break, I hope you could ask some specific questions concerning these maps. We will rise until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You are allowed to ask some leading questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, those of us who are experts in the legal profession obviously see certain things in a different way compared to you, but try to be as specific as possible. I put to you as specific questions as I can and please answer as much to the point as possible. Now, this ethnic map, could you explain the colours and what was the purpose for this -- for which the map was drafted? Is it for the census or whatever?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at the very beginning of my testimony, I feel the need to explain certain matters for, if I don't do it now, later on the map will remain unclear to many an observer. The map is the fruit and result of the different developments and trends in the development of the three constitutive peoples. Now, it has been said, and this is true indeed, that Bosnia-Herzegovina, in all Yugoslavia, had the most dynamic growth of its population among all the federal units of the former Yugoslavia. Now, this statement alone says nothing about this country. This most dynamic growth is in fact the result of the diversities and the disparities that are obvious when comparing the constitutive peoples with another one. If this growth is then reduced to the three constituent people, then the demographic value of this growth becomes quite a different matter. To put it in terms of interpretation, it would sound as following: Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1981, in 1991, for example, had a higher growth of the Muslim population than was the percentage growth in its total population. Of course, you might be flabbergasted by this statement, and you might not be satisfied with it. Therefore, may I be allowed to add a sentence or two because this might lead us to it a more concise and briefer answer later on? Namely, the growth of a population is the result of birth, deaths and migrations. How, then, is it possible for one of the constituent peoples to have a higher growth than the entire country, comprising three constituent peoples? This is possible in the following manner. One people grew faster on the basis of higher births and migration of population from other entities, while in other parts, birth rates were lower and people were leaving these individual territories. This, however, is only part of the answer, why are some peoples having lower birth rates? Why in one entity are people leaving the territory more often than in others. If we take just one example, if we take the Croats and compare them to Muslims, there were twice-higher birth rates among the Muslim population and six-fold migration from the Croat populated territories compared to the Muslims. In other words, quantities, figures, percentages, are disrupted and through this disruption, the quality of this sensitive social fabric is also being disrupted. And if this sensitive social fabric, which lives in circumstances of an underdeveloped economy, you try dividing the little riches you have among more people than in the past, then obviously nobody will be satisfied. If those who are more productive get less, then this will give rise to the feeling of injustice and inequality of rights and inequality is in fact, in my view the result of insufficiently developed economies. Hence, one can draw the following relevant conclusion, as far as I can see matters. Once you have little and you're trying to divide this to many, then everybody will be dissatisfied. If you are trying to raise funds for a budget, then you have a limited source of funds, obviously, and those who are bigger in number will then decide on ways and means in which the budget will be distributed. And then step by step, dissatisfaction escalates and this dissatisfaction gives rise to social frustrations, social clashes which usually are referred to as national, religious or Balkan syndromes. When I say that some were leaving the country of birth during peace time, this is usually just an expression, and this is of course viewed from the point of view of a demographer, so this is an expression of their dissatisfaction at home. And I told you what later on this may lead into. So throughout the 20th century, the demographic competition, if I my use this word, in the relevant territory has been going on and on, and resulting in the fact that the majority population became the Serbs, and in the second half of the 20th century, the majority population would become the Muslims. The smallest number would, in the structure of population, be Croats who are now pushed into a situation of expecting what is next to come. So in my people, in my local culture, usually people tend to use all sorts of sayings. One of them is, a donkey that has to compete with two horses will find it very difficult to win in the race. I hope I haven't insulted either the donkeys or the horses or my fellow citizens who are not of my ethnic background. This is why I think that the map in front of you is the context within which we need to seek answers to the question why the country I come from has been sort of exposed to a growing feeling of dissatisfaction which unfortunately culminates in a tragedy affecting one and all. Within the context of the counsel's question, I will show you a map --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What is the number of this map?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: 406. Now, this map, 406, is -- was drafted five years prior to the former map. Obviously this map is the result of the war that raged in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For the sake of simplification, I should like to outline the context and not the result, the outcome because the outcome is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. obviously very tragic as is illustrated by this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, you said this map 406 was drafted five years prior to the former map. I notice that this map was drafted in 1996, and the previous one is 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a mistake made by your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. This was a mistake on my part. I wanted to conclude with one sentence. Any simplification whatsoever in -- even in terms of cartography, when my country is concerned, has no practical value whatsoever. All averages, given the history of my country, and given the economy and the culture, such as it has prevailed, have resulted in this demographic structure. Averages on the one hand is one matter, and as we usually put it, without superimposing upon the averages, demographic cultural, economic situations will only bring us further from an insight into the context that I have just been describing. I know I can't continue but this is possibly the situation which breeds the crisis that culminated in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very briefly, we have this map in front of us. Could you explain the -- this Trial Chamber, what is the difference comparing 1991, where we have a very picturesque map compared to 1996, where we have a rather more homogeneous structure?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Trying to answer your question, well, I have already explained the situation to a certain extent. Ethnic cleansing caused by migration of the Serbs and the Croats throughout the 20th century was the result of these migrations. The war, however, only expedited this sort of development. And the consequence of these developments is the map in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us what do the colours depict?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, the red colour, this was a long time ago, in 1996. Changes took place in this map because the red colour shrank and the red colour depicts the Croats, except in the part of the map which is Bosanski Drvar, Bosanski Grahovo and Glamoc. Now, why did this happen I'll tell you later. The green colour depicts the Muslims or the Bosniaks, who now chose their new name and the blue colour stands for the Serbs. In other words we are here facing a process which is the consequence of the war but if we examine this at the level of information that is available internationally, particularly within the framework of the UNHCR and on the basis of some data and information which have to do with the census for the purpose of election, one can conclude the following. The return of the Muslims was more intensive than the return of the Croats to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what is particularly important in the entity which is called the federation, the Muslims, that used to live in current Republika Srpska territory are now returning to the federation. In this manner, I'm afraid, we are now in fact concreting the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina such as you can see on this map. In other words, there is less and less, territory available for Croats to return to Central Bosnia and also to Republika Srpska and this applies also to the Muslims returning back. Obviously these are the conclusions based on sources that are not credible. Some newspapers and publications were used. Unfortunately, after the war, a proper census, population census, could not be carried out. However, it would be an avoidable and a very much necessary type of research for anybody to be able to see how this war ravaged country's structure has been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have two more questions. The first is the following. You as an expert and under the patronage of the United Nations participated in the drafting and designing of the maps and also in relation to the peace agreements reached under the patronage of the international community. Why were your maps or maps such as the one I have in front of me, were usually made by minority population representatives and not by the majority population representatives?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I emphasised this in my introductory testimony, namely that I was a member of the BH delegation experts attending the London conference held in 1992 on the former Yugoslavia. Furthermore, I also emphasised that I participated in the preparation and drafting of professional foundations for the political agreements to be later on reached within the framework of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, you gave me -- this is probably the single original available -- of the Vance-Owen Plan signed in New York on the 26th, I think, or 23rd of March, 1993, containing original signatures of all participants but Mr. Karadzic's signature. Perhaps it would be a good idea to put this on the ELMO to comment on this document. But could you tell us something? Why parts with a majority population of one ethnic background and other ethnic background and then we will come to Mostar where the Prosecution says one thing, the Defence didn't have the necessary answers to come back to my question, why do parts of municipalities with this minority and that majority are important? Could you please explain to us what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I'll be very glad to do that but I'm afraid that I'll be penalised for a lengthy answer. First, it is true that I was an expert who participated in the preparation of the Vance-Owen Plan. Here you have the signatures, but one, who will then be added after the Athens and Pale and other events. Unfortunately, this political project was not of long lifespan. Here I use the colours to show the border lines that had at that time been agreed. It is obvious that the current shape and structure of my country is quite different. Your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Majority-minority. Why did all the maps, as part of international agreements, depart from this fact?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: The current appearance of my country will indeed reflect the principal criterion on the basis of which it was shaped and drafted. The majority Serb territories are the Republika Srpska and the majority Muslim-Croat are the federation. Does this not speak for itself? Namely that the ethnic criterion was the decisive one, was the predominant one. One remark: Participating in this whole affair, under the patronage of the United Nations, participating in the Vienna negotiations as a foundation for the Dayton peace agreements, the application of this criterion resulted in the following: 58-42 for the benefit of the federation entities comprising the federation. Even today, I'm not quite sure why 51 to 49 ratio was eventually adopted. On the basis of this criterion, there is the difference of 7 percentage points to the detriment of the federation. Now, speaking about the majority population and the minority population, I must admit one thing to you. These notions, and these concepts, in the past, before the war, were not topical, were not operative concepts. In fact, the first maps after the war, that you had seen at the very beginning of my testimony show, that this will eventually become a very frequent criterion used in negotiations, peace plans, and in the final organisation and structuring of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Naturally one could say that at that time two entities it were in fact available or proposed. Reminding you of the minority-majority criterion which was particularly topical and interesting in the first stage of the war, through the development of the so-called Serb autonomous provinces and Serb regions, which at that time were sending a signal of warning also through the political terminology used, that this, as it turned out to be, was an introduction to the war based on this principle. Unfortunately to this very date, everything changed in Bosnia-Herzegovina except municipalities as such, which are almost half a century old. By the way, if, in a semi-literate society this criterion was not heeded, the criterion which 50 years later, when literacy has prevailed, will become the criterion on which the country will be -- on the basis of which the country will be organised. In other words, the municipal, legal and actual predominance of the majority over the others did occur. Why is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this important? This is important in terms of the distribution of authority and budgetary funds. Let me also say the following: Today, we know that before the war, 44 per cent of the Bosnia-Herzegovina population were Muslims, 31 per cent were the Serbs, and 17 per cent, maybe a little more, were the Croats. However, given the demographic fact, given the migration of the Muslims to Bosnia, the Bosnian electorate was much smaller, given their age structure, than was their overall percentage in the total population. In fact it was about 38 per cent. The Serbs were demographically an older group, so 36 per cent of the Serbs were part of the electorate. And for the Croats the relevant number was 22 per cent. This interesting demographic statistics could be used by you to question this country's organisation. Given the plebiscite, given the referendum, and Serbs' abstention from the referendum, given the fact that only two entities ethnicities participated in the referendum, namely only the Muslims and the Croats, and to go on with the specific features of this country, it goes without saying that two peoples cannot recognise their own country on their own, unless this is a combination of the Serbs and the Muslims who are larger in number. Well, I'm not a legal expert myself. However, I know that my country did not have enough demographic clout to be recognised internationally, but to my satisfaction, the international community did recognise it officially in the end. You need to in fact hear also this post factum statements. Of course they were printed and published in my book on time but what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's give the Chamber another, only original version with the signatures of all the participants in the Vienna talks. That was on the 11 May, 1994, the Bosnian delegation was led by Mr. Haris Silajdzic and Mr. Kresimir Zubak was the leader of the Croatian delegation. That was on the eve of the Dayton Accords, and it was the introduction to the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you please give us your brief comment on that document? And then we will move on to the topic of the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to my very limited material competences, can I ask Madam Registrar to copy this huge format and shrink it into a smaller size? I could not find a photocopier where I could do it?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: You could see the signatures of the delegations of the Bosniak and the Croatian delegations in Vienna in the first half of May, 1994. We, after the Washington Agreements, we were happy, we were satisfied that the war was finally over and we did not hide that. In a certain way, we, if you will allow me to express my emotions, we were happy that the tragedy was behind us, and we, bearing in mind the criteria, which still leave a lot of room for discussion, we established -- we came up with a joint proposal that was in a conversation with the mediation of the contact group, and that was in the conversation with the delegation of the Serbian people, that was just another attempt to organise the area to the benefit of all the concerned peoples, all the three peoples. Obviously the Dayton peace accords resulted in something very different. Again, I would like to say the municipality which was 50 years old was not respected, especially when it came to the minority. So the structure of municipalities did not respect the national structure. I'm not saying this because I think that my state has been turned into a ghetto or that the ghettoisation of my state was attempted with that, but because this was an attempts to avoid the direct clash that could have broken out between the peoples. I still believe that this is just a transitional need for us to try and learn how to live with each other in order to be able to live together. There is a term which is used in my state, and that term is "peaceful Bosnia." In this country, you have heard a lot from many people, I'm sure that this term has been used, and I'm sure that you know that it is very hard to translate this term, but part of the answer lies in that term. What I'm saying is that people did live next to each other in their municipalities, in their parishes, in their religious communities. I am using the terms with religious denotation reflecting the territorial division of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, in English, the word is going to be the same, the religious municipalities are called in different ways in different languages.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Zupa, Z-U-P-A is a Catholic municipality. Parohija, P-A-R-O-H-I-J-A, is an orthodox municipality, where the orthodox population prevails. Dzemat, D-Z-E-M-A-T , is also a territorial unit where the Muslim population lives and where Islam confession is practised. So this is where Bosnia indeed was peaceful. However, melting -- a melting pot never was something that really existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was very much the result of the situation that prevailed after the year 1945. The melting pot did not -- did not pass the test of time. When I say that, I mean particularly that the semi-literate people, with over 50 per cent rate of illiteracy in the state, was not the best resource, the best medium, who could be said with too much credibility, "as of yesterday there is no God." I witnessed that myself. I know my father, my mother, my grandfather, my grandmother, still believe, and in my family I could not believe that there was no God, as I was told, and I believe that this is a normal human right that belongs to every confession and every nation. This is equally Muslim, Catholic and Orthodox right. Throughout my life, I convinced myself that this shouldn't bother those who do not have religion in their souls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Professor, I am moving on to my last question. I'll try to put it to you in the following way: The demographic and territorial terms, what is the city of Mostar, and particularly, the census 1991, and are there any scientific methods that you have used throughout your research that could shed some light on the allegation that we have heard in this courtroom, that there was ethnic cleansing of any people in the city of Mostar? Was any people ethnically cleansed in the city of Mostar? And can this be either proved or denied based on scientific facts?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I have to be very brief --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think goes beyond the scope on which this witness has been tendered. He's been tendered as a demographer and not on conclusions whether ethnic cleansing occurred and I think Your Honours will have to decide that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that you have to rephrase your question. You could ask this witness to show the different statistics before the war, after the war, but this witness is certainly not a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not surprised with such a position that we just heard from the Prosecution. Before I had my first conversation with the professor, I was an absolute layperson and I was very ignorant when I started reading books and when I got the first explanation from the professor, the title of the expert work is the state between ethnic cleansing in peace and the ethnic cleansing in war. Demography is the science that deals with that topic, based on the scientific facts. This is the essence of this science. And here we have the scientist who can explain this. He can give us scientific evidence to illustrate the changes that took place in municipalities, villages and towns. I am now looking for the scientific explanation of what has really happened. I'm looking for scientific truth from this professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. In very brief terms, in front of you, you have the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, covering the periods from censuses 1990 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not catch these. The interpreter apologises, the interpreter did not catch the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can we have the number of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: 408. The black areas -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry for warning you so often. Can you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: The black areas, in other words municipalities, show the demographic drain of the Croatian majority in the administrative, territorial division, as the result of various demographic processes prevailing amongst the three peoples. And that in turn is the result, not only of demographic, but also social, cultural, economic and other reasons based on which one population develops. May I say at this point that while Germany is looking after over 20 per cent of its aged population, at the same time, the underdeveloped India has over 36 per cent of school-age population. China, which has several billions of inhabitants is struggling how to manage families and how to reduce families to have only one or two children, because it is overpopulated. In the area where I live, the consequences are what they are because of the reasons that I have mentioned. The demographic drain results in a social losses. The sensitive tissue, the sensitive fabric of Bosnia-Herzegovina is very complex and it had to learn about its complexities in order to it be able to manage them. Why this did not happen is a different story. And that is why social collisions based on all different differences sometimes can live together and sometimes they escalate. When we say that everything is changing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, professor, I'm sorry to interrupt you but the Defence counsel was asking a very specific question, which is concentrated on one city, which this Trial Chamber is most interested in. That is in Mostar. Tell me something about the change of the populations in Mostar before the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When I was reading your book, you called Mostar a "Mostar case," as a typical example of political manipulation. So I found that in your book. Can I please now ask you to explain to all of us here in the courtroom what has happened with Mostar to this very day?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: If you would allow me, Your Honours, I would like to say that it is very difficult to explain my country and what it is all about with just simple yes or no. I started to interpret this map, but I am going to remove her from the ELMO now, but I will to have go back to that map again. Now I am showing you the Exhibit 409, the map 409, which shows the territorial position and the territorial area of the administrative unit of Mostar throughout the past 100 years, between 1879 and 1991. It is clear that the differences in the size of this administrative unit, and its shape, and in its colour -- when I say shape, this shows changes over time, and the colour shows the predominant people, the people predominating at the time. It is clear that until the year 1961, the red colour predominates and the light red colour predominates and that in 1971, 1981, 1991, there is a change and there is a zigzag change in line. The green colour here depicts the majority Muslim population. And this is what I have spoken about so far, the notion of majority and the notion of minority is not just a demographic and statistical notion but it is the overall social issue and that in the development of one society encumbered by the political ideology, this issue can be manipulated and abused. This can be done by way of assessing things, of giving privileges. I don't have a proper answer to the question as to how can one people, that is in more specific terms, the Croatian people, can have the following characteristics? How can it be the least numerous, the most prone to emigration? And we all know that it is very hard to leave one's own house, one's own home, how can it be the least organised and at the same time how can it be the most educated and also at the same time how can it occupy the least number of positions in the so-called public sector, which entitled to those who are employed there to a number of privileges in terms of acquiring all the necessary resources of one's existence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let's move on to 1991. I'm going to give you this fact. Here, we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, this witness was called as a demographer, not as a politician or an apologist for the Croatian nation or culture. Now, control your expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Judge Clark, I did not know how wide, how broad, is the scope of this science, demography. Demography has to have all this data available in order to come up with certain assessments. Here in the courtroom we heard that in 1991, there were Muslims, Serbs and Croats in the city. And we heard some figures, some statistical figures. Can you please give us who was the minority, majority, or whatever people in the city of Mostar? How was it organised? What was the majority population in the city or in the municipality of Mostar? We have been confused on that. Can you please try to shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I really apologise if anybody think that is I'm advocating anybody. This is an omission on my part. But this is what I usually tell my students in order to give them the essence of the context, because people do not propagate out of the context. The municipality of Mostar had its national composition in 1991 that national composition shows a Muslim prevalence. In this specific case, the Muslim population prevailed by 0.6 over the Croatian population. However, when it comes to the municipality of Mostar, very often there are numerous such examples that the municipality of Mostar is manipulated, has been manipulated at the detriment, to the detriment of the factual truth, and the factual truth is that every municipality, including Mostar, has its own centre, its own nucleus. The nucleus or the centre of this municipality was 70 per cent of the municipal population. Now, what is the manipulation all about? The manipulation consisted in the fact that the municipal structure served to show a message to the world that Muslims prevailed in the city of Mostar and that Mostar was a predominantly Muslim city. I'm not disputing that. I'm not saying that it wasn't. The city of Mostar was at the same time a Jewish town, although in statistical terms, there are only 14 Jews living. But if we are going to be statistically precise, then the city of Mostar has the prevailing Croat population. Why am I saying this? It is very important that the general public is not deceived, that the general public understands the facts for what they are without purporting to hurt anybody. The city of Mostar, or the city area of Mostar, unlike the municipality of Mostar, is the central focal point of what is the main part of my expert opinion. I have to say another thing, again based on statistics. There is no doubt that -- and I can corroborate that with the papers that I have in my brief case. I can quote all the statistical data to you if you're interested in hearing them. But to my mind, it is much more important for me to say, to give you the approximate figures to illustrate what I am talking about. The city of Mostar is on a river and the river has its left bank and its right bank, and if we look at that statistics, then I, as an expert, was very much impressed and very much surprised with the following fact. As long ago as 1953, statistics, as everywhere else in the world, even then followed the recommendations of the UN statistical organisation. In my expert work, I said that what is in -- what is incompatible with the 1991 census, what is not compatible with the 1991 census. The state offered the general public data on all the inhabited municipalities, including the municipality of Mostar, in a rather correct way. However, the question is raised here. I asked that question myself. This data was pretty much hidden from me. Why would a state such as it was, why did it publish the data in 1961, 1971, 1981, only for one part of the city of Mostar? That is for five city neighbourhoods. And at the same time, it did not publish the data on the entire territory of the city of Mostar, and which it was as long ago as in 1953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which five municipalities were those? Which five neighbourhoods were those? Five out of how many? For a better understanding, five neighbourhoods in Mostar of how many of them in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I said that, I'll correct Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. myself. Only five municipalities -- for only five municipalities, the statistical data were published, and there were seven others which were recognised in 1953. So that's five out of 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, professor. It is very difficult for all of us to follow you. First you have to slow down. Secondly, you have to explain yourself thoroughly. Not even our Honourable Judges, not even my learned friends can follow you. I can do it a little bit better. When you say the city of Mostar, can you please give us its composition?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Can I use some statistical data if I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't want to lose the bit. You were saying something very interesting, professor. As long ago as 1953 statistics, you looked at it and you were really surprised. You never told us what surprised you in the 1953 statistics, and you seemed to have gone astray and we are still waiting to find out. You were talking about the city being divided into two banks and it sounded as if some part of the city was never included in the census, but we've lost that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having noticed that. I obviously was under the impression that you understand me. I'll go back. I'll follow up on your question, and I'll try to be -- to say that in simpler terms. My surprise was a statistical surprise which consisted of the following. Every city, including the city of Mostar, has its territorial organisation, has its territory which is considered to be the territory of that city and which is composed of some neighbourhoods which are more or less densely populated. The official statistics role is to take into account that during the census and publicise the data for the territory for which -- to which the census is applied.
