And they did that only for the year 1953. Despite the fact that in the meantime, the territory of the city of Mostar has grown. In 1961, 1971, 1981, the official statistics has excluded some of its neighbourhoods, and that is what I found so surprising, because earlier on, I must admit, I was not interested in that. I did not pay any attention to that. Why didn't I pay any attention to that? If I -- if I live somewhere for 30 years and if I wanted to study the local demographics of any such town or if I wanted to study the local demographics of one part of Sarajevo I would have found it very hard to do if I based that research on the official statistics, because such statistical data were not published, although the -- all the censuses did collect all that data. There are various reasons to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? I think what Judge Diarra and I wanted to know was: Was the area, which was described as the city of Mostar in 1953, larger, therefore, than the area which was described as the city of Mostar for purposes of census in 1961, 1971 and 1981? Or was there a fraud perpetrated on the people who were reading the statistics? In other words, they pretended the area was the same but in fact it had shrunk? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly what I am trying to say. With your permission, Your Honours, I have this folder with me with all the data and I can put them on the ELMO for you to see what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see there is no objections from the Prosecution. You may use it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott? Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no objection, Your Honour, but I think at this point, the Chamber will note that I've been very quiet this afternoon. I just want to note for the record at this point we are now being, the Prosecution has now been confronted with an abundance of information since this testimony started which we've never seen, in fact many of which we have not seen, because it hasn't been provided to us. I'm sure the Chamber will understand we will not in a position to conduct a full cross-examination of this witness so perhaps he may be brought back in the future when we have a better chance to see the information, including the information the witness is now pulling out of his brief case for the first time, which has never been provided to the Prosecution. I'm sure we will not be able to finish our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will take note of what you said. But we'll see after the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, if the professor could just show us the size of the municipality of Mostar for census purposes in 1953 and then how it shrunk and thereafter, but what I'd really like to know is what happened to the missing people? Did they get attached to some other place or did they just disappear into a black hole?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. That was in fact my principal question but it is very difficult for me to guide the professor. One reason being my ignorance, and another reason being that the professor finds it difficult to follow our legal mind and direction, because your question, in fact, would have been the crux of my questions, and the witness prepared a special study, a research, for the whole of Mostar, for the UNHCR from house address numbers to the house councils, et cetera. We just have to it be a bit patient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When trying to explain why the municipalities persisted for such a long period of time I should have said the following: Mostar is the only city which throughout its entire history, in the censuses, until 1963, was the only city that changed its size, its territory, the only city, the city of Mostar, that was give and new structure, through the Dayton Accords. And that's a fact. When mentioning the migration of the people from the right bank of the river to the left bank of the river in my expert opinion, I failed to understand the legislator. In fact I was not interested in the legislators line of thinking why they kept doing it in the case of Mostar from one census to another. However what was the consequence of this territorial change is something that I tried to show to you. I will now, to be more specific as possible, I'll show you the foundations on which I arrived at the conclusions that I'm sharing here with you today. Could somebody help me, please? Because I can't manipulate with this equipment myself. I apologise. So if you would be kind enough to have a look at this, I will read out the columns. On the top, it says, the population according to the ethnic structure in terms of local communities of the municipality of Mostar. These are the lists that were usually drafted in the course of all censuses. This is one stage in the entire census procedure. What I wanted to emphasise, however, is the following: All stages, given the high costs of censuses, are not being published. So some territorial units, such as the local communities, which are parts of the -- of a town, are very difficult to understand. The data are very difficult to gather unless you have an insight into the statistical office's detailed records. This might sound funny to you but this is the fact. I'm not going to lament this fact but this has to do with the so-called politically sensitive issue of the ethnic question in Yugoslavia. However, I, as a scientist always say the sensitive issues will become even more sensitive unless we understand the degree of sensitivity of that issue and the trend of either growing or declining sensitivity. Here you have all sorts of signs that I made in order to be able to establish the statistical accuracy and nothing else. So these are the so-called local communities in the city of Mostar. Now, I will show you another original list, which refers to Mostar in 1991. Now, first column says, "Area," then municipality, city of Mostar, if we go down, then the municipality of Mostar, left bank and right bank. And having seen these data, one can conclude the following. The city of Mostar, such as it is shown through these statistical data, had, in 1991, 92.768 citizens. Croats, as I mentioned before, live inside the city and they were the most populace in the city, and not in the municipality, 3.266. The next number, 8.085, is the number of Muslims. Then 17.413, the number of Serbs. And then we have 12.222, which is the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of those who expressed themselves as Yugoslavs and 2.587 are the so-called others. We were now reading the line which is called Mostar city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear I'm sure the witness apparently made a mistake when the number that came across in the transcript for the Muslim number was 8.085. I believe on his document, if it's correct, it says 28.185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that. I'll ask the witness to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. Scott. I can't guarantee that I can read these figures well but I'm always -- I always stand to be corrected. Now, if we view now the city of Mostar and single out these data from the statistics that are officially available, only in the statistical offices, then we can make the conclusions that I described in my previous statements. At that time, the city of Mostar has its right bank and its left bank, which, in a way, is indicative of the structure of the city. This city, in other words, it would be good if I had my expert opinion now in my hands. To be as correct and precise as possible, at least as far as statistical data show and statistical data is the only data that I can really believe, because these are official records concerning the data of any country, including mine. Now, we are talking about the following matter. The city of Mostar should have shown, in terms of statistics, data, and in terms of the neighbourhoods, in my expert study -- this is page 18 in the original, I don't know which is the relevant page in translation. So the statistics in 1953, with your permission, should have been the following, and with your permission, I'll read out the statistics for the sake of accuracy. Let us immediately proceed to the bottom of this page, which reads as follows. "The city of Mostar in terms of its ethnic structure, of its population is a heterogeneous city. However, the Croats are the most populate ethnicity. Throughout the first and thorough administrative and territorial restructuring in the territory of Herzegovina, which took place in 1953, so after the second world war, when my country had about 50 per cent of its entire population illiterate, the city of Mostar comprised the neighbourhoods of Brankovac, Carina, Cernica, Donja Mahala, Luka, Zahum -- and the neighbourhoods of Cim, Ilici, Rodoc, Vihovici [phoen], Rastani and Vrapcici. It is difficult for me to find everything. I'll just continue. It is difficult to find a rational or reasonable answer to the question why official statistics throughout the censuses that followed, that I had already mentioned, showed the number and the structure of the so-called city population for the first group of neighbourhoods only, and/or for only some -- I am coming to the end -- some parts of the territory of the city of Mostar. In the meantime, i.e. through the following 50 years, obviously, Mostar went beyond its former territorial boundaries and the statistical data blindly followed the city of Mostar focusing only upon the first aforementioned group of neighbourhoods. Here, in the city of Mostar, not knowing about it, for 40 years, two cities grew and developed next to one another. One which is real and much bigger, and the other one which is the official statistical city of Mostar, which was boiled down to a small group of its neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, could you please tell us on which page in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll check it during the break, Your Honours. I would like to conclude with my examination until the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 24, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So shall we break now, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest that I complete with my part, because we haven't come as far as 1993 and 1994. In fact, I would prefer to hand the professor over to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But professor can you tell us whether the population changes took place in Mostar through what we in lay terms refer to ethnic cleansing? Were there really any migrations or any changes in the population structure? Did you through your scientific method find out that some people were missing?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I tried to share with this Trial Chamber the information based on official statistical data provided by the former republics and current states' official statistical offices. Of course it's difficult for me to answer this question but I thought that we have to use some of the official statistical data to show that there were errors and mistakes made even by the official statistical offices. So that my testimony, in answering your question, could be related to what has been used as the foundation of my scientific assessment concerning the credibility of the sources that I had to search for so that I could, in either absolute or at least approximate terms, discuss the issues at stake. All other sources -- and they are abundant indeed -- excited me, not through their credibility, but rather through -- how to put it without resorting to it an apology -- which, as I said before, led the public at large to make false, erroneous conclusions, and that in some people, even thwarted the image and the picture of a -- of the specific area, thus, in fact, giving a distorted picture to the public at large of the territory in question. Now, in this context, what I tried to show to you in fact was my attempt to answer your question. There were changes that took place, and I would have to resort to my credible sources to be able to give you a more detailed and precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will -- with your permission, Your Honours, ask the professor to sort out his documents during the break because the time is really running out. We already spent two hours. But after the break, perhaps the witness would be able to answer the question in a more concise manner. And then I would put my final questions, which I'm sure everybody would be interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Maybe just one question before the break: Professor, do you have any statistical data as to how many Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina have left since 1991 for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Shall I be brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes. If you can.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: About 316.000 Croats born in Bosnia-Herzegovina are living in the Republic of Croatia, according to the 1991 census. But these are figures and data that I gave you in my expert opinion. I have a feeling that you are verifying my knowledge, my awareness of the data that I had supplied to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not testing you at all. We just have to be very brief and specific. We are looking forward to your expert answers because we are lay persons and we are looking forward to you to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I am willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you then perhaps during the break prepare the data as to the changes in Mostar and possible ethnic cleansing developments in Mostar at any point in time? And now we have to go and have a break for the sake of our interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I also hope that if this document has been sorted out, as well as the document used by this witness before, it could be photocopied and furnished to us because they are new documents. So we will rise until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, you heard my question before the break. I hope that we can now focus upon this question and issue, and answer as briefly and to the point as possible.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Having reviewed the official statistics concerning Mostar, the municipality of Mostar, and the city of Mostar, as explained by me before, I'd like to draw the following conclusions. In the 1991 census, the municipality of Mostar had a majority population of Muslims comprising 34.8 per cent, then followed by the Croat population with 33.8 per cent, and with your permission, for the time being, I will not consider the Serbs, the Yugoslavs and the category "others." In this same census, the city of Mostar has a predominant Croat population, 34.9 per cent to be more specific, followed by Muslims, accounting for 30.4 per cent. The examined left and right bank of the city shows in these two peoples the following breakdown: Left bank, 14.4 per cent are Croats and 43.6 per cent are Muslims. Now, the right bank: 41.5 per cent Croats and 26.1 per cent are Muslims. Your question, counsel, the way I construed it, refers to the following question: On the basis of my expert opinion, did any changes take place and/or any ethnic cleansing to which either ethnicity would be exposed? Now, statistical data shows the following. Before coming to that. Let me emphasise that so far, I used in my interpretation official statistical data. However, corrected in terms of the data that refer to the city of Mostar, for reasons explained before. To be able to answer your question, I need to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the following fact. In the period following 1991, as already described by me on one occasion, there was no further census of the population. At the same time, it seems to me, I also added that since 1991, to this very day, all -- I underline "all" -- people, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside the country, have been involved in all sorts of statistical operations. This is why I tend to be very careful whenever using or interpreting statistical data of whatever source. However, to be credible in the answer to the question put to me, I also need to share with the Trial Chamber the following facts. Given the fact that there was no official census carried out, and given the fact that no official censuses are -- have been announced for the near future, certain assessments can and have to be made on the basis of the data available, and to be able to answer your question, I resorted to some sources which have put up the data for quite different purposes. I have all these sources in my brief case. However, I limit myself to the most important ones only. One, there is -- there are report prepared by the refugee office titled "Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna." And the title of the report in fact is the following, "The report on the moment of displaced persons and refugees in the municipality of Mostar from the start of the war, in brackets, the 6th of April, 1992, closed brackets, to the end of the year 1993, including relevant specific data." The authors are Mirko Alilovic and Ante Aleksic. I also used other sources which compiled data for other purposes. I'm specifically referring to the municipal council of the municipality of Mostar, the welfare centre of the municipality of Mostar, which, for its own purposes, was in charge of the accommodation of the displaced persons and refugees, and the provision of humanitarian aid. The weekly report for the 12th -- 23rd of December, 1994, and the 5th of April, 1995. The next source is the municipal council of the municipality of Mostar, the department for social welfare and family care, the report broken down in terms of local communities which shows the population on the day of 28th of May, 1994, the 26th of June, 1994, the 29th of July, 1994, the 26th of August, 1994, the 29th of August, 1994, the 30th of September, 1994, and the 28th of October, 1994. These are my basic sources, together with a gamut of other individual sources, I was able to use a large number of data, statistical information, and media sources, and having been involved for 30 years in matters that have to do with statistics, I could consider these to be very credible sources for my expert work. In addition to these, in the meantime, I came across other sources but I will not mention them here. Yet they can be made available to the Trial Chamber. If we know that ethnic cleansing or the notion of ethnic cleansing, the way I understand it, implies an organised persecution of those of other confessions, then, within this context, I will once again have to resort to the earlier tables. Statistical data shows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for the interruption. I can't, of course, completely forecast what's going to happen in the next couple of moments but based on what the witness said just a moment ago I'm concerned again we are getting beyond the scope of demography and into other polemics and the witness just said a moment ago, "The notion of ethnic cleansing, the way I understand it, implies an organised persecution." Now I think comments on organised persecution go beyond the scope of his testimony as a demographer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you came here to testify as a witness of demographics, not as a legal expert. We want to know the changes of the population statistics, but this is not your testimony for the reason of these changes. Yes, you may proceed, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On the right bank of the river, according to the 1991 census, there were 18.286 Muslims and 10.782 Serbs and 10.034 others. I said earlier that there were 29.095 Croats. Based on the sources that I have just quoted to you, we can see that, from the beginning of the conflict between Muslims and Croats, as is usually said that took place on the right banks -- bank of the river, throughout the conflict, there were between 8.000 and 11.000 Muslims, which is over one half of their total number. I have to add something else here. The entire right bank, neither during the conflict nor at any other time, was under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. Local community Cernica, which you can see highlighted, and the largest part of Zahum were under the control of the Muslim army. This is according to my free interpretation. At the same time, in accordance with the sources that I have personally analysed, in Croatia, there were 2.423 registered refugees from Mostar, and they were Muslims. There was a lot more of them in total. When the data from the sources are interpreted, and when that number of the refugee population is added to the figure, or better still, if that is subtracted from the total number of Muslims, I'm talking just about one people, in order to make it easier for me to explain my total findings, then the figure of 18.286 Muslims has to be reduced by that number. If we add to that the fact that the conflict -- because there are no other credible sources -- that because of the conflict, the men of both peoples, after the conflict most probably left the area with their respective armies, the armies to which they had belonged, we will come to the fact that among the men, there were 3.500 such individuals in the Muslim population. If we also say that before the conflict, a large number of the population in Mostar had escaped, had fled, because that is the sad fact in every war, and also that a large number of Muslims from other areas of Herzegovina, Eastern Herzegovina, came to Mostar, and another most probable fact that a number, a large number, of Serbs, after the liberation of Mostar, left Mostar, then my answer to your question would be, in terms of statistics, in the way I interpret facts and in the way I arrived at this conclusion, so the statistics do not corroborate the widely publicised thing, and that is, again, if, in the city of Mostar, which is corroborated by some other data that I'm aware of, so if there were over 10.000 Croats in the city of Mostar, who came from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, most probably from the left bank of the River Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Neretva, and if in the city, according to the official states, there were 7.650 Croats, then it is most probable that after the conflict, after the end of the conflict, that a number of them moved from Jablanica and Konjic, but what was carried by the media, I would agree with that, it is very difficult to find sources which would show how many Croats remained on the left bank. And another thing, about 70 per cent of the Serbs who -- that is 2.5 to 3.000 Serbs who remained in Mostar after the liberation of Mostar, so I'm talking about 2.500 to 3.000 Serbs, that is 70 per cent of their total number, throughout the war to this very day, have lived on the western -- in the western part of Mostar. In my brief case, I have a lot of documents showing the names, the numbers of identity cards, of those people who are -- were not Catholics, who were not Croats, who receive pensions, who received humanitarian aid, and who, throughout the conflict, to this very day, have lived there. I live and work at the university, where there are Muslims and Serbs among the faculty, among the students, not to the same extent as there were before the war, and there are people working in the media, in the health care, who are Serbs or Muslims. So I believe that one should use documents to refute allegations from other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, professor, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can just organise our documents for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These are for distribution to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Before Mr. Scott starts, can I ask a question, professor? Can I just ask a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. You've explained very ably that a thesis that is widely held is incorrect, and you've given us the reasons why but you haven't actually identified what the widely held wrong thesis is. Is it widely held because nobody I think has said that so far, that there is a Muslim majority in Mostar? Is that the thesis that you intend to refute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are absolutely correct, and I believe that I have provided you with ample information based on the official statistics that corroborate that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The reason I asked you the question, professor is that I don't believe anybody has given that evidence in this trial so far. We haven't heard anything about the change of population since 1991. It just hasn't come into this trial at all, because we understood that there had never been a census.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, you are right. And I accept your information with satisfaction. That is true. However, I am bringing you all the impressions from the country where I live. Everybody has talked about that, about the fact that the city of Mostar is a Muslim city. And I have never denied that. But my subtitle says, "A Muslim town with a predominant Croat majority." These two things do not go together. I want to be precise when I say something. But when you are talking to a large number of people, and when you are not saying the truth, that large number of people, the mass, starts accepting your lies. And then we arrive at something that is called brainwashing. And this is the answer to some questions regarding the behaviour of the masses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Professor, we only have about approximately 45 minutes left tonight, and I will admit to having some prepared questions that I want to get to eventually, but before I do, I would just like to cover some of the things that have come up just today in the course of your testimony, just to clarify a number of things. First of all, if you have your bundle of maps or diagrams before you, if I can ask you to look at those for a moment, Exhibit 403, the one you told us about in connection with the -- trying not to it use a provocative word, but I think by your own admission it included some political commentary. Exhibit 403, what was the source of information that you used to characterise the various parts of the map, the municipalities or other parts of the map that you've characterised in terms of in the black and white we can only see various shades of black, white and grey I suppose but what was the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I have to repeat to the Honourable Chamber what is important for this map. This is the map that reflects my mood. That is my protest against the aggression that Europe had to stop. This map kept me in the basements of Sarajevo because this is my personal interpretation. This is what I saw. I just wanted to be, so to speak, credible in the sense of saying that, as a human being, I felt this foreboding of the tragedy, and the tragedy struck the places characterised by black. I do not pretend that this is a source but this is just my understanding where places are being shelled, where women are being raped. This is what the radio, television and newspapers were allowed to carry, and this is what I felt sitting in the basement of my Sarajevo flat for the first seven to eight months of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I think all of us in the courtroom can understand the sort of emotional feelings of going through this kind of experience would cause, and I don't mean to quarrel with you about that at this moment but we can understand, then, Exhibit 4 o 03 to basically be a kind of emotional presentation if you will, not based on any particular statistics or demographic information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, and I did not want to hide my emotions but I do not pretend to say anything else but admit that I'm just a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if I can direct your attention -- it's not the next numerically, but in the order in which we went through them on direct examination, I believe it's 410. I would like to ask you a similar question about that, sir. Can you tell us the source and the data -- the source of the information or data you used to draw certain conclusions or give certain colours or shading to the map that is shown on Exhibit 410? I should say I suppose for the record to be clear, D1/410.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have the short, medium or long version of my answer. The longest version is in my book. The following I need to mention, because it is important. I was a very fruitful journalist during 1991 and 1992, and my subjects mostly related to this topic, and I -- I relied on all the information that was available at the time in Sarajevo. I was also a member of the Crisis Staff which provided for the refugees and the -- I was also an expert of the first Ministry of social welfare. I con--

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise but I do want to cover some ground this evening. I appreciate what you told us so far but let me be very specific, please. Just you're a demographer, you're told us you're a scientist, so I'm asking for very technical information, if you will, almost as a footnote to a report. If you can just tell us the source, the actual sources from which you drew the data that's reflected on this map. Was it statistical information from the statistical office of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was it from some non-profit organisation? Can you just tell us very specifically the names of the sources from which you drew this information?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was the Crisis Staff in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which followed official information on the number of killed, the dead, injured, and so on and so forth, and of course, it was the key source for this map, the newspapers were published, the radio worked, the television worked for a long time afterwards and the ambition of this map was to show the Sarajevo in which I lived, and also to show where the area -- war struck areas were, where the war-free areas were in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the conclusion of my expert study was that the war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was waged in the areas which were not predominated by the Serbs, in order to make room for those who were supposed to be ethnically cleansed from the so-called Republika Srpska. So the purpose of this map is just to provide the reader of the newspaper with the information on where the war was waged at the beginning of 1991 and the source was the Crisis Staff for refugees. I don't know exactly the name of that institution at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is again should not be interpreted as indicating demographic information of the sort that is reflected in some of our other maps but again this was your interpretation of where some of the worst conflict had happened up to that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: If I may say, demographic sources are official statistics, and they use all the other sources that may serve to explain a certain demographic phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. On Exhibit 404, please, which is -- appears to be a newspaper article, I basically am just interested in the item that is attributed by your name and in the document, it is the lower right corner approximately. If the booths have that -- if the translation booths have that, perhaps they could simply read that so that those of us who don't read Croatian could know what this says. And then maybe I'll have a question about it and maybe I won't?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comments we don't have it translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I can inquire of the booths, you don't have the B/C/S original in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do have the B/C/S original, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it possible for someone in the B/C/S booth just to it read that to us and translate that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "In his numerous writings, Ante Markotic in Oslobodjenje gave the most competent picture of the multi-national, multi-religious, multi-cultural being in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the most credible evidence on the deep division and of the fates of its peoples."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. And this was published on the 30th of August, 1992; is that correct, sir? I'm looking at the handwritten date that someone, perhaps yourself, has written in to the left of this -- on the left side of the page, or approximately the middle of the page. Do you see that? 30 -- it appears to be something like an abbreviation, Oslob 30/8, 1992. Is that the date of this publication?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the date and Oslob is the abbreviation for Oslobodjenje and the text was written by somebody who was -- who awarded the golden medal to me as one of the three winners of that medal. In this paper, but I would like to say that I have never got this medal because at the time when this happened, I was at the London conference. But my friends gave me this paper, and I keep it as my document, as part of my documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where is that publication, excuse me, where is this publication published, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Oslobodjenje on the 30 August, 1992. That is at the Oslobodjenja newspaper from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to look, then, to the next exhibit, 405, going to continue, sir, to ask you similar questions about a number of these documents and on this Exhibit 405, the multi-coloured map, again, can you again tell us, please, the data, the source of the data on which this chart was prepared?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Certainly, I can. In short, this is statistical bulletin, the preliminary results of the census on the 31st of March, 1991. The statistical bulletin, I can provide you with, or I can find the number of its issue, and if I may add to that, according to my information, this is the most widely published map of Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1991, to this very day, and if copyrights have at all been respected, I would now be very rich rather than a very poor professor who hasn't received his salary of 500 Euro for third month in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry for that, sir. Maybe Mr. Krsnik can help you with this claim of some sort. The bar graph, the vertical bars -- sorry, Your Honour, it's getting late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The United Nations are in charge of that, I believe. There is no pay for justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as I interpret this and I may be absolutely wrong, so assist us, please, within the municipalities, there also appear these vertical coloured bars, again, blue, green and red. Unless I missed it, I didn't get an interpretation of what do the bars reflect as apart from the colour of the municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: You can see in the keys, if I may say so, if you understand, I know that it is in my language so it's very difficult for you to understand it, it may be a problem, the -- this host of squares, I can see them on my screen, should provide you with an answer to the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just assist you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: These are municipalities with an absolute majority, we are talking about the three peoples, and an absolute majority can be treated in different ways. It is very difficult to establish a statistical threshold in a map that can give you just the basic outlines. I have spoken about that in length because I assumed that I may be put some more questions of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you but my specific question, I think I can't speak for the rest of the courtroom but I believe I understand the colours of the municipalities and the percentages that are reflected. You're absolutely right there is a legend and down in the lower right corner much that diagram, there is one, the vertical box that has the number 36 in it, but again I apologise for not being able to read Croatian. My question again is, what specifically is being represented or illustrated by those vertical bars?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Only vertical? Only vertical bars? Or anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me help you, let me take an example. In Foca, if you can find the municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which is down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the image in the ELMO should be on the other side. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can find the municipality of Foca, sir, which is basically a light green colour, then in that municipality, there is a blue box which has a number in it. It appears to have a number at the top of the bar but at least I can't read that number. What does that vertical bar represent?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I wanted to read the number. However, I can't see it too well. There is a technical deformity here. That's why I -- my answer is that this municipality has a relative Muslim majority, in which the other people, the second in size, is the Serb people. The light green is 62 and the column, the vertical bar, gives you the percentage of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can help you. I can read it, it says 44 on that bar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that means that the number on the light green is different. It cannot be 62 either by the colour -- because nothing can go beyond 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think perhaps you've taken as far as we can but perhaps we will come back do it. I'm not sure. Well, you would agree, wouldn't you, that your chart, this 405, would indicate then that, for instance, Jablanica, was a substantially -- substantial Muslim majority municipality? And again if I can read it, I think it says 72 per cent or has the number 72. Konjic has approximately somewhere around 55, 55 per cent Muslim majority. Gornji Vakuf has approximately 56 per cent Muslim majority. And the municipalities of Mostar and Stolac are reflected as being mixed Muslim-Croat municipalities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: If you have read the numbers well, then this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in terms of some of the information that the Chamber will have heard a fair amount of evidence about in the past months, the predominant areas of red, either completely red or mixtures of red, if I can put it that way, are in Herzegovina, which is on the Croatian border -- on the Southwest Croatian border, excuse me, southwest border of Bosnia-Herzegovina which runs along the Croatian border which -- will are a number of municipalities that are completely red. That would be the single largest concentration obviously of Croats, of the Croat population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but Your Honours, I've already drawn your attention to some possible erroneous conclusions. If you simply identify a map in this way. I have it in my hands and I can show it to you. If you remember, in Kalinovik municipality near Sarajevo that was the example I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, for present purposes, I'm just simply trying to indicate, just perhaps for more basic purposes for the courtroom, if there are three primary areas, you have the area we just described which is Western Herzegovina. There is somewhat of a higher concentration of red up at the upper part what might be called the northeast corner of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's an area, just so the Chamber can associate it with a name it may have heard, that was also called the Posavina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then the prime -- the principally mixed area in the middle, the middle that has diagonal markings a mixture of red and green, is what we typically refer to it as Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of orientation, both the first and the second and the third were right, but if you think that Western Herzegovina is west of Medjugorje then it is an artificial division. Geography does not recognise anything but firm features like a mountain, a river, as division points or division lines between the areas. And the municipalities, the municipality, very simplified here is very deceiving, because in spatial terms, in area terms a much larger Kalinovik with only 600.000 inhabitants gives a false image with regard to Sarajevo, and if you look at the map, the impression you will receive, that there are much more Serbs in Kalinovik than in Mostar which is a deception, very well known deception. Once again, a map is not a reliable source of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, sir, and again, you're just for the moment going beyond the point that I'm just trying to make. My point is much more basic than that. Now, let me -- let me go away from these charts for a moment to ask you a couple of questions, other questions, about your background. In the period roughly from 1990 to 1995, sir, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Since 1988, I have not been a member of any political party, either since 1988 or 1989. And even until then, in the period prior to these two years, I was a member of a political party but not through my free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And have you at any time held -- I think you said you were the assistant deputy mayor of Sarajevo. If I heard it correctly. But have you held any other elected or appointed positions in any sort of governmental organisation or structure?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: It is with pleasure that I mentioned that I was deputy mayor of the city of Sarajevo, but could you please be more specific? What period does your question refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well I'll use the same period I used before, from approximately 1990 to 1995. Did you hold any elective or appointive offices during that time, positions during that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I had a function which was the councillor in the Office of the President of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I did it from December, 1993 until approximately March, 1994. -- furthermore, I was the deputy minister in the government of Herceg-Bosna since September, 1974 -- I apologise, not 1974 -- 1994, until December, that is until the Dayton Accords were reached in the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you about both of those a bit more, please. When you say you were a councillor to the President, as of the end of 1993, that was Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did he continue to be the President during that approximate four or five month period until March of 1994, or was that about the time that Mr. Boban was replaced?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you about something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you answer my question? Please answer my question first. I'll give you an opportunity but please answer my question first. Was that -- throughout that period was it Mate Boban or was that about the time that he was being replaced?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I was hospitalised in a hospital in Zagreb, and I couldn't tell you a lot. In fact, I learned about it after my surgery, namely that I was appointed councillor, possibly as an expert participating in the Vance-Owen Plan. In fact, this was a consequence of my participation in the Vance-Owen Plan which had happened at the beginning of this year. I apologise but I am a bit tired, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But -- and who appointed you to that position as councillor to the President?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: While I was hospitalised, my brother came to visit me and he told me that he read about this somewhere in a newspaper. I assume that the person who was in charge of that in the office, but how and who, I never asked about. When I was told this, I thought that those in positions of authority can either send me to the front line or use me as an expert, which would have been much more sensible, and I myself would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, is it fair to say, just to hopefully cut this short, it was Mate Boban who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also said you held a position of deputy minister in the government of Herceg-Bosna from approximately September of 1994 to December, 1995. When you say deputy minister, are you saying -- when you say minister, are you talking about being a member of parliament, a legislative body, or did you have some ministerial function in what we might call the executive part of the government?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: No. I told you what I was. I was appointed by Mr. Kresimir Zubak, most probably because of my participation in the Vienna talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me when you say deputy minister. I'm just not sure what that means? What was the deputy minister, do you mean deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: In the government of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, I was a deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in -- and what was your area, the Deputy Minister of the Interior, the Deputy Minister of defence? What were you Deputy Minister of?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: For international cooperation and cooperation between republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you have a copy of your report with you, -- in front of you, but if I can have the usher show you possible Exhibit D1/317 which is the report that was filed in this case, D1/317?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I have the report in my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, that may assist you as well. Please keep that handy but just for the record, I just want the marked version also to be in front of you, so there is no question about that. You've been now handed, I think I can see from here, D1/317. Now if you have a Croatian language version available to you, you're certainly welcome to use it. But if I can direct your attention to the first page, sir, the overview, if you will, your background, what might be called at least in part a CV, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've got it. I have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just -- I don't know, do you read some English, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: It would be easier if I had it in my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me, perhaps let me just assist you. I have just one question about it at this point. I'm just curious, sir, if you can assist the Chamber in this way, when you're background was listed and it was listed that you had been a deputy mayor of the city of Sarajevo, did it not occur to you to indicate that you had also held these very senior positions in the government of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Now, I could have written ten pages of my CV, but in my life until the war, I thought that these were matters of interest. I mentioned here that I participated in the London conference, the Vance-Owen Plan, the Vienna talks. I chose a few pieces of information. But that doesn't imply that I did not hold any position in the period until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, let me continue, please. You chose the information to provide to these Judges and you chose not to provide information that reflected -- that indicated that you held two very senior positions in the government of Herceg-Bosna, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. I do not deny these two positions, but I don't think these were that senior positions, given my involvement in the events mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: For example, I never attended a single session of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you held these positions, in particular when you were a councillor to Mate Boban, I'm going back now to the -- excuse me, I'm going back now to Exhibit 405, the chart with -- the multi-coloured chart we were looking at a few minutes ago, Exhibit 405, please, D1/405, my question to you, sir, if you have that, is this: Based on the additional background that we now have, do you recall any discussion with Mr. Boban or other people around him about the issue presented by the fact that there was either a majority or very substantial Muslim populations in the municipality of Jablanica, Konjic, Gornji Vakuf, Mostar and Stolac, which was all within the boundaries of what was claimed to be Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: My answer would be no, because at that time, I was undergoing post-surgery treatment of about four months, but what you have referred to as Herceg-Bosna, here I'd like to add an opinion of my own. Knowing this case, I have noticed that false interpretations have been offered here of the notion of Herceg-Bosna in territorial terms. In the course of international talks, I came across some maps which could not be considered acceptable under any circumstances. For example --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not referring to any other maps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, can I finish my question first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me hear Defence counsel. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness be allowed to explain? Because the manner in which this cross-examination is conducted will not allow us to learn anything from the professor but will only be offered those answers that the learned friend is asking for. If a question was put to the witness, why wouldn't the witness be allowed to answer? Questions were raised in connection with the municipalities of Jablanica, Konjic, Gornji Vakuf, et cetera, in terms of the ethnic structure. Would the witness please be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we have limited time at our disposal. We only want to hear what we are interested in. I believe this witness has answered that question by the first few sentences of his answer. Yes, Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. If -- sorry, I'm trying to ask this question in a way that will not be -- belabour it. You were appointed this position with Mate Boban as his councillor, and did you not know it to be an issue, not only among Mr. Boban but among the senior Bosnian Croat leadership, certainly the circles he moved in, and apparently at least to some extent that you moved in, that it was a problem to establish a consolidated area of contiguous borders for Herceg-Bosna when you had these substantial Muslim areas inside them? Wasn't that something that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, I'd like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that I am not Bosnian Croat. I am a Croat from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Furthermore, I wish to emphasise the fact that it was in the hospital that I learned about my appointment to this position, and during my post-operative care, which lasted for almost the rest of 1994, there simply was no opportunity and time for me to be involved in these issues that the Prosecutor has been referring to. There are documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of the -- some of the demographic information that you told us, what's happened in the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you tended to focus, if I heard you correctly, among other things, on two primary -- two principal phenomena. The fact is apparently, if I don't use exactly your words forgive me, but that the birth rate of Muslims was much higher than the Croats and that the Croat, the rate of Croat immigration, that is emigration out of the country, was substantially higher, resulting in the fact that as the Muslim population became larger, the Croat population was becoming smaller. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: With the full appreciation of your erroneous notions, the gist of it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll accept the gist. Based on that, sir, is it change -- this situation, is it your recommendation, or would it be your policy suggestion, that Croats should be prohibited from emigrating and Muslims should be limited in the number of children they can have?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: When talking about such complex states as is Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the notion of policy can also be found in demography, in terms of population policy. In other words, I was not involved in policies here but if this were the interest of my state, which has to be heeded, I'd prefer to develop a study which would answer the question how to maintain the ethnic balance in such a complex country. I therefore reject the very notion of my political involvement. I was participating in this only as a professional and Bosnia-Herzegovina can't have too many professionals, including those covering my area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, but if I read your report correctly, and I've listened to your testimony today, it appears to be -- and counsel can ask other questions, the Judges can ask their questions, of their understanding of what you're saying but my understanding is again, two of the principal factors in these demographic shifts are a higher Muslim birth rate and much higher rate of Croat emigration. Sir, neither of those factors are related to what we might call war crimes, were they or are they?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have understood it well. But I'd like to offer my personal comment. In statistical terms, that's true, but demography and statistics are not serving their own purpose only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just so the record is clear, Mr. President, it will be my last question for the evening. You've made several references to being involved in the peace processes under the patronage of the UN. Just so there is no misunderstanding, sir, you're not suggesting that you were employed by or part of the United Nations, are you?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: No. Under no circumstances. I can only say that I received the UN grant and I spent this UN grant programme in Moscow, in 1980, focusing upon the study of population and development.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. I was talking about the times you told us you were involved in the peace processes and the truth of the matter is, sir, and it's nothing necessarily wrong with that but you were part of the Croat delegation, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTE MARKOTIC
utterances.text: I was part of Bosnia Herzegovinian and Croatian delegation. In the course of the peace talks. In my CV I mentioned it and I also orally repeated those involvements which I considered to be the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll stop there for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one second of your time, if I may, once the witness has left the trial -- the courtroom. I need with your attention for just a second after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm sorry that we could not finish your testimony today. We have to keep you here for another day at least. So you have to remember that you are still under the oath. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony today and do not let anybody talk to you about it. You understand that? Thank you very much. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely understood, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik? We will see how long a second is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second. Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 7.07 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of June, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
